skill.name: wsdiscovery
skill.description: WS-Discovery protocol scanner for discovering and enumerating ONVIF cameras and IoT devices on the network. Use when you need to discover ONVIF devices, cameras, or WS-Discovery enabled equipment on a network.
skill.summary: Discover and enumerate ONVIF cameras and other WS-Discovery devices on authorized networks.
skill.author: BrownFineSecurity

security_audit.summary: The skill intentionally executes WS-Discovery scans and supports host or multicast discovery. Markdown backticks and private example addresses are mostly scanner false positives, but authorization safeguards are absent.

remediation.issue: The workflow does not require confirmation that the target is owned or authorized.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit authorization and an approved scope before scanning. Refuse public, third-party, or unapproved targets.

remediation.issue: The command examples accept a user-supplied hostname or IP address.
remediation.suggestion: Validate targets as hostnames or IP addresses and pass them as separate arguments without shell interpolation.

remediation.issue: The multicast example can query every compatible device on the local network.
remediation.suggestion: Explain the multicast scope and prefer a specific approved host unless broad discovery is explicitly authorized.

content.value_statement: Finding ONVIF cameras and compatible IoT devices manually is slow. This skill guides WS-Discovery scans and explains device metadata in clear formats.
actual_capabilities: Guides wsdiscovery scans against a specified hostname or IP address.
Supports text, JSON, quiet, and verbose XML output workflows.
Identifies addresses, device UUIDs, types, manufacturers, models, versions, serial numbers, and locations.
Uses the standard WS-Discovery multicast address for authorized local discovery.
Explains service endpoints and metadata that can support later ONVIF testing.
limitations: Requires the wsdiscovery command from the iothackbot bin directory.
Finds only reachable devices that support and advertise through WS-Discovery.
Does not authenticate to, exploit, or reconfigure discovered devices.
Does not include a built-in check that confirms target ownership or authorization.

use_cases.title: Inventory Security Cameras
use_cases.description: Discover approved ONVIF cameras and record their models, firmware versions, serial numbers, and service endpoints.

use_cases.title: Troubleshoot Device Discovery
use_cases.description: Use verbose responses to investigate why an authorized camera or recorder is missing from management software.

use_cases.title: Inspect IoT Metadata
use_cases.description: Review WS-Discovery types, scopes, device identifiers, and XAddr services during integration testing.

prompt_templates.title: Discover One Device
prompt_templates.prompt: Confirm that {target} is authorized, then run a text WS-Discovery scan. Summarize each responding device and its service endpoints.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner scan of one known host

prompt_templates.title: Create a Device Inventory
prompt_templates.prompt: Scan {authorized_target} with JSON output. Present a concise inventory of addresses, models, firmware versions, serial numbers, and XAddr services.
prompt_templates.scenario: Structured inventory for an approved target

prompt_templates.title: Diagnose Discovery Responses
prompt_templates.prompt: Run a verbose WS-Discovery scan against {authorized_target}. Explain the returned XML fields and identify missing or inconsistent ONVIF metadata.

prompt_templates.title: Assess Authorized Multicast Discovery
prompt_templates.prompt: Within the approved local network, query 239.255.255.250. Group responding devices by type and flag outdated firmware or incomplete metadata for review.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced assessment of an authorized device segment

output_examples.input: Scan an authorized camera at 192.168.1.100 using text output.
output: One WS-Discovery endpoint responded at the requested address.
The summary lists its device type, identifier, model details, metadata version, and management service endpoint.

output_examples.input: Investigate why an approved recorder does not appear in discovery.
output: No WS-Discovery response was received from the target.
Check routing, multicast filtering, firewall rules, device discovery settings, and WS-Discovery support.

output_examples.input: Summarize an authorized local multicast discovery scan.
output_examples.output: The inventory groups responding cameras, recorders, printers, and media devices by address, type, manufacturer, model, firmware, and service endpoint.

best_practices: Confirm ownership, written authorization, and target scope before every scan.
Start with a specific host and use multicast only when broad local discovery is approved.
Protect verbose responses and inventories because they can contain serial numbers, locations, firmware details, and management endpoints.
anti_patterns: Do not scan public, third-party, or unapproved addresses.
Do not insert untrusted target text into a shell command without validation and argument separation.
Do not publish verbose XML or device inventories that expose sensitive infrastructure details.

faq.question: What devices can this skill discover?
faq.answer: It can discover reachable cameras, recorders, printers, and IoT devices that advertise through WS-Discovery.

faq.question: Does it require network access?
faq.answer: Yes. The agent must reach the authorized target or local multicast network.

faq.question: Which output formats are available?
faq.answer: The documented command supports text, JSON, quiet, and verbose XML-oriented workflows.

faq.question: Can it discover every camera?
faq.answer: No. Cameras must support WS-Discovery, enable advertisements, and be reachable through current network controls.

faq.question: Does it change device settings?
faq.answer: No. The documented workflow discovers and reports metadata without authenticating or changing configuration.

faq.question: Is multicast discovery safe to run anywhere?
faq.answer: No. Use multicast only on a local network where broad device discovery is explicitly authorized.
